scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Fann at-Tanbura originated as a communal ritual tradition in the Arab states of the Persian Gulf, especially within Bahrain, Kuwait, and Oman.
The genre developed through historical cultural connections with East Africa, embedding African-derived ritual practices into the musical fabric of Eastern Arabia.
Historically, it was closely associated with the Zār spiritual tradition and utilized primarily for healing and ceremonial rites.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally, Fann at-Tanbura was performed as a sacred healing ritual within the Zār tradition, where music and dance were deployed to treat ailments and induce spiritual trances.
In contemporary society, it has largely evolved into a valued form of public musical and dance heritage, performed during cultural celebrations, national festivals, and folk music showcases.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Men and women participate together in the singing and dancing.
The movement relies on rhythmic body shifts, hip sways, and steps that actuate the manjur—an apron strung with goat hooves attached around the waist.
As dancers move, the striking of the hooves against each other generates a sharp, rustling percussion that aligns with the drums and lyre.
Watch for Manjur Shaking.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The musical ensemble is anchored by the tanbura, a bowl lyre that plays a central role in driving the melody and rhythm.
Accompanying the lyre are several traditional drums and the manjur, a percussive body-worn instrument constructed from a large number of goat hooves attached to a waist apron.
Listen for the tanbura, manjur, drums.

A dense polyrhythmic soundscape dominated by the resonant plucking of the tanbura lyre, layered drum patterns, group chorus singing, and the sharp, continuous metallic-like rattling of goat hooves from the manjur apron.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: A primary functional element of the costume is the manjur, a large apron fitted with numerous goat hooves worn wrapped around the performer's waist.

The dance was historically conducted in private or semi-private ritual spaces for Zār healing ceremonies, whereas modern performances take place on public stages, cultural centers, and festival grounds throughout the Gulf region.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The genre is documented across the Arab states of the Persian Gulf, with prominent localized traditions and performance groups found in Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, and the United Arab Emirates (such as performance groups in Sharjah).
Fann at-Tanbura forms a subclass of Arabic folk music and Arab folk dance, carrying historical links to African musical heritage in the Persian Gulf and the broader Zār ritual complex.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Fann at-Tanbura is historically linked to the Zār spiritual healing ritual and trance practices. Performers and observers should treat its ritual contexts and sacred heritage with cultural respect.
